#### Cancer is falling nationwide. Except in Iowa.

Cancer rates are declining across most of the United States. But Iowa is moving in the opposite direction. Iowa now has one of the nation's highest cancer incidence rates and is one of only three states where rates continue to rise. So what's different about Iowa? Nick El Hajj, reporter for the Des Moines Register, joins The Excerpt to discuss the theories researchers are investigating, from drinking water and nitrate pollution to radon exposure and other environmental factors. ##### Description

Cancer rates are declining across most of the United States. But Iowa is moving in the opposite direction. Iowa now has one of the nation's highest cancer incidence rates and is one of only three states where rates continue to rise. So what's different about Iowa? Nick El Hajj, reporter for the Des Moines Register, joins The Excerpt to discuss the theories researchers are investigating, from drinking water and nitrate pollution to radon exposure and other environmental factors. He also shares the stories of Iowa families searching for answers.

Read more: https://tinyurl.com/4zj9fkaf

##### Transcript

###### Iowa's rising cancer crisis

**0:04** · Most of us think about cancer risk in terms of genetics or lifestyle [music] choices, but how much could your zip code matter? In Iowa, that question is no longer abstract. It's being asked in hospitals, in farm towns, and by families who are looking for answers.

**0:21** · I'm Dana Taylor, and this is [music] The Excerpt. Join me to dig into the question of why Iowa's cancer rates are rising as the nation's fall. Is Nick El-Hajj, reporter with the Des Moines Register. It's good to speak with you.

**0:34** · Hi, Dana. Thank you for having me.

**0:36** · Nick, when we talk about cancer risk, how much can where you live actually matter?

**0:42** · Yeah, I quite a bit, actually, Dana.

**0:45** · Geography, or where you live, is essentially a proxy for everything that comes with living in a place. What you breathe, what you drink, where you work, and simply what you're exposed to over a lifetime. And those differences can be enormous sometimes. And that holds true on the national level, but also on the state level.

**1:16** · Why has Iowa become such an important place for researchers and public health officials to watch?

**1:23** · Iowa has really become one of the country's biggest cancer outliers. It not only ranks second in the nation for cancer incidence, but it is one of only three states where incidence is still rising. We're talking about 21,700 Iowans who are expected to be diagnosed with cancer in 2026 alone. And about 6,400 Iowans who will die from cancer. And that's because Kentucky is getting better while Iowa is getting worse.

###### Statewide impact and scale

**2:14** · And you can see that pressure on the ground. Cass Health quadrupled the size of its cancer center in 2022. Four years later, in 2026, they are already struggling to meet demand again. And people are again having to wait for months to see a specialist.

**2:40** · And so all these numbers and concerns have just made Iowa this laboratory for asking, "What are we missing?"

**2:51** · You know, one of the striking things is how many Iowans say cancer has touched nearly every family they know. That's stunning. Can you talk about how that shaped communities there? I mean, those are big numbers that you just gave me, but how is that affecting communities in Iowa?

**3:09** · Yeah, they're not You know, Iowans, from my experience, especially farmers and and rural Iowans, can often be very stoic in nature. They take things in stride. They push and persevere. But sitting around kitchen tables in in some of these rural communities, there becomes evident this seismic shift in how cancer is being perceived. For years, cancer was almost treated as as a way of life.

###### Community perspective

**3:46** · But now the toll and the suffering have become too overwhelming and too visible to ignore. And there is real pain and there's a real anger and hunger and demand for answers. I spoke with Maureen Reeves Horsley, a nurse in Palo Alto County, Iowa, which is the county with the second highest rate in the state. It used to have the highest in the state.

**4:10** · She told me she could name at least 40 people, 4 0, 40 people who have had cancer or had died from it within her vicinity. That is not normal. And the story repeats across Iowa. You'd be hard-pressed to find anyone in the state who doesn't know someone who has had cancer or who has died from it. And that is not normal.

**4:39** · And Maureen described this crisis to me, I I think rather eloquently, as this sleeping giant that has been dormant for decades, but that has now been poked. And it's become impossible to turn a blind eye to it and to the sheer despair that exists in Iowa when it comes to cancer at the moment.

**5:03** · Well, a big focus here is on water quality.

###### Environmental factors

**5:07** · Why have nitrates become such a major concern?

**5:10** · Iowa has staggering levels of nitrate pollution. And And this has been the case for for decades. Des Moines is home to the world's biggest nitrate removal facility. And research time after time has shown that those nitrates primarily come from the billions of pounds of fertilizer and the hundreds of billions of pounds of animal manure applied on Iowa fields.

**5:42** · Whatever is is over-applied, either stays in the soil or it leaches through that soil and it goes into the rivers, which then supply the same water we all drink.

**5:57** · Why is agriculture seen as a possible contributor? What does the evidence actually show and what's still uncertain?

**6:05** · Then our researchers are really playing this elimination game.

**6:11** · Uh there's three buckets. If you take behavioral factors like drinking and smoking, that's the first bucket. Those are high in Iowa. They explain a large share of the elevated incidence, but not the whole picture because compared to neighboring states with with similar behavioral factors, Iowa is is still high. Iowa has the highest levels of radon in the country, a radioactive natural gas that seeps into homes and causes lung cancer. About 84% of the state is farmland.

**6:41** · There are pesticides and herbicides being sprayed across millions of acres. And research, time after time, has shown that agriculture is causing nation-leading chemical levels in Iowa.

**7:00** · If we take one pollutant, nitrate, research has shown that nitrate levels as as low as 3 mg per liter in drinking water can contribute to an increased cancer risk. And by the way, that level is is three times lower than the current federal limit, which is 10, that water utilities are required to abide by.

**7:22** · So you essentially you end up in a situation where those elevated nitrate levels and that level means from 2021 to 2023, you have 1.2 million Iowans, over a million Iowans, estimated to have been served by public water systems that have recorded a nitrate test above that level of three, that cancer-causing level. So, when you're trying to understand what makes Iowa different environmentally, agriculture is obviously going to be part of that conversation.

**7:57** · That begs the question, why is it so difficult to prove that a specific environmental exposure caused someone's cancer?

###### Challenges in research


**8:05** · Cancer can be and is so overwhelming.

**8:10** · Usually, it it doesn't work like an infectious disease, where you can trace one exposure to one outcome. It can take decades between an exposure and a diagnosis. And during those decades, a person can accumulate well, thousands of other exposures alongside genetics, alongside lifestyle, and alongside random mutations. And pinpointing where in that chain things are going wrong is an enormous task.

**8:46** · What are the biggest unanswered questions researchers are still trying to solve then?

**8:51** · The biggest one, I think it's still the most basic one.

**8:55** · Um why Iowa?

**8:58** · Why did Iowa break away from the national trend around 2013? Because Iowa used to follow the national trend, which is declining. The national average is declining. Why did Iowa in 2013 start going up while the US average kept going down? And now we're at this point where they're so far apart. Why is the cancer rate still rising here when it is falling in most of the country?

**9:22** · And why does Iowa still stand out even compared with nearby states that look a lot like it?

**9:29** · Nicky spoke to a lot of families who still want answers.

###### Personal stories of survival

**9:33** · What struck you the most in these conversations?

**9:37** · I sat down with patients like Lavonne Schroeder. Lavonne has been battling the same cancer, ovarian cancer, for the past 23 years. She's been sent home to die three times already. And yet, here she still was, settled into one of those recliners at the cancer center. And another round of chemotherapy flowing into her veins. Three years ago, while fighting her own cancer, Lavonne cared for her husband and their farm home until he died from spinal cord cancer.

**10:22** · And after all these years fighting, she told me she was tired. She said she was at peace with whatever the doctors were going to tell her. That she was at peace with whatever may happen this next year. The takeaway I got here, and from this whole reporting, is just that the sheer toll cancer has taken on Lavonne's life, and on the lives of thousands of Iowans, [music] can be unimaginable.

**10:57** · Nick Colangelo is a reporter with the Des Moines Register, part of the USA Today Network. Thank you so much for sharing your reporting here, Nick.

**11:04** · My pleasure. Thank you for having me, Dana.

**11:07** · Our stories come from USA Today journalists across the country. I'm Dana Taylor. Tap subscribe for more [music] from The Excerpt.

About this episode: Biosolids created by the wastewater treatment process are useful fertilizers in agriculture, but they often contain chemical compounds from the pharmaceutical and personal care products we send down our drains. In this episode: Researcher Carsten Prasse details new findings that suggest that fungi could reduce our risk of exposure to these compounds in our drinking water and food. Guest: Carsten Prasse, PhD, MSc, is an associate professor of Environmental Health and Engineering at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, where he studies organic contaminants in the urban water cycle and their impact on environmental and human health. Host:  Stephanie Desmon, MA, is a former journalist, author, and the director of public relations and communications for the Johns Hopkins Center for Communication Programs. #### Good Shit - How Humanure Could Save Agriculture—and the Planet

![Good Shit: How Humanure Could Save Agriculture—and the Planet](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1ff45e75d8ccf0c5243333cd98)

**Duration:** 00:51:07

**Released:** 2023

**Series:** Gastropod

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2bB44RWKrgs1jhylH1NBtL)

For most of us, when we sit on the porcelain throne to drop the deuce, priority number one is flushing and never having to think about it again. But it might be time to rethink our stink: all around the world, people are talking about using human waste for good, applying it as fertilizer to grow our food instead of just washing it down the miles of pipes that undergird urban sewage systems. "Ew" is a common response, along with "yuck!" Is using poop to grow food a good idea—or even safe? We’re getting our shit together to find out! On this episode of Gastropod, how human waste went from being so valuable you could go to jail for stealing it, to causing such a stench it shut down Parliament in Victorian London and led to the invention of the modern sewage system—and why figuring out how to start saving our poop (and pee!) once again could give us cleaner energy, healthier waterways, and lots of delicious food. Listen in now: if you like to eat, it's time to start giving a crap about your crap. Learn more about your ad choices. Visit podcastchoices.com/adchoices

:::

In this episode, we sit down with Professor Meredith Niles to explore how climate-friendly agriculture—from methane-reducing rice irrigation to no-till farming—is actually a quiet powerhouse for public health. While traditional environmental messaging has hit a wall, shifting the narrative to human health benefits (like keeping heavy metals out of baby food and clearing our air) might be the key to finally getting farmers, consumers and policymakers on board. It’s time to take off the carbon goggles and look at the health potential of sustainable farming.

#### How Can Iowa’s Agriculture Adapt To Climate Threats?

Climate change is having a profound effect on agriculture. Farmers over the past decade have faced intensifying drought and heat stress on crops, leading many to wonder, what will agriculture look like 50 years from now?In May, at SciFri Live at Iowa State University in Ames, Iowa, Ira Flatow discussed the future of agriculture, and potential solutions to these problems, from innovative farming techniques, to ensuring that Iowa’s farmers of color have the resources they need to succeed. He was joined by Todd Western III, a sixth-generation Iowan farmer with Western Family Farms and senior donor advisor at Greater Twin Cities United Way, and Dr. Patrick Schnable, a distinguished professor at Iowa State University and co-founder of Dryland Genetics.Transcripts for each segment will be available after the show airs on sciencefriday.com. Call us: 877-472-4374 Hosted by Simplecast, an AdsWizz company. See pcm.adswizz.com for information about our collection and use of personal data for advertising.

It was an eye-opening discussion. Have a listen.

Here to tell us about how they do all of that are my guests. Let me introduce them to you. Todd Western III, a sixth-generation Iowan farmer and Senior Donor Advisor at Greater Twin Cities United Way, and Dr. Patrick Schnabel, a distinguished professor at Iowa State University and co-founder of Dryland Genetics. Welcome, all of you, to Science Friday.

TODD WESTERN III: Thank you.

PATRICK SCHNABEL: Thank you.

\[APPLAUSE\]

IRA FLATOW: Yes.

\[APPLAUSE\]

PATRICK SCHNABEL: Right.

And he did a great deal of research about the crop. Came back for Christmas time. We celebrated Christmas together. And we spent the entire week talking about proso millet.

It’s the most water-efficient crop on the planet. It uses less water for each pound of grain produced. And that’s how it was able to do this. It survived, and it actually produced grain without being watered for a month or two.

IRA FLATOW: Can I buy this millet on a store shelves?

And so from 1974, that’s when we took over the farm. Because at that point, my dad, when he got out of the army, he was the first Black supervisor at John Deere in 1968, where he worked for 41 years at John Deere.

And then tragedy strikes in 2008. My father was training for his 13th Chicago Marathon, and he had a bicycle accident. And so he was one week from his birthday and nine months from retirement. And yeah, it was rough. And so that put a big hole in our family. And so it was in July.

And so about three weeks after the funeral, you got all the shock and awe and disbelief. And then me and my brothers looked at each other and was like, holy crap, there’s still a crop in the field. Like, we got to–

So at that point, you think, OK, now, where did dad put the keys? What did he do with this? How did he do this? How did he do this? And so you’re thinking this is going to happen 20 years from now.

And so we banded together, and we got that crop out of the field. And so from 2008 to 2015, we were pretty much on autopilot. And we just did whatever dad did. And so whatever dad did, that’s what we did.

So in 2015, what we realized is we have to be better stewards of the land, and we have to create better efficiencies in the farm. So my mom comes out of retirement. Now, you have to understand, my mom is like 5 foot 4, but walks 8 foot tall. So she is a go-getter.

And now, remember, my mom was a city girl from Chicago. She knows nothing about farming. She knows how to help, but she knows nothing about farming. So in 2015, seeing the need to improve the soil health of our farm, she jumps full bore into farming and learning agriculture.

She’s a woman of faith. And so because of her faith, God led that path, and they put a lot of angels in her path. And she really was the heroine there, where she created the relationships with all the state agencies– FSA, USDA, NRCS, Iowa State Extension office. They were all very welcoming to her and helped her understand the programs. And that’s when we found out about regenerative agriculture.

IRA FLATOW: Well, let me stop you there because I get asked more times by people who come up to me and say, I want to pitch a story to you. Why don’t you talk about regenerative agriculture? And so now, I’ve got the guy sitting in the chair. Tell me how you do that and what that is.

TODD WESTERN III: So regenerative agriculture– first of all, it’s up and coming. It’s not well known, especially in 2015 when we tried to get into it. Thankfully, Iowa State Extension Office and all the great offices helped us get into it.

And what we do is– there’s many variations of it. But the core of it is we do no till, which, by the way, is not fun. When you grow up tilling, and you want to tear up the dirt.

IRA FLATOW: It means you don’t plow the–

TODD WESTERN III: We don’t plow. We don’t disc. We don’t do anything. That was a huge disappointment with regenerative agriculture, let me tell you.

\[LAUGHTER\]

So now we got–

IRA FLATOW: How do you plant the seeds if you don’t plow? Tell me.

TODD WESTERN III: I’ll tell you.

IRA FLATOW: Yeah. Go in the weeds on this, so to speak. Go in– you know.

TODD WESTERN III: So the main thing to remember, and they’ll probably agree with this, the soil doesn’t need your help. The soil has its own mechanism. The soil has its own time to do things. We just do it as humans to get it bigger, better, and greener.

And so what we do is we do no till. We do cereal rye cover crops, and we do nutrient management, and we let Mother Earth do the rest. And so what happens is, is when you plant that cereal rye, it holds that earth together. It creates a mechanism, it creates the biomass in there. It creates the worms to get in there. And the earth does its magic. And so by the time you go to plant it, it’s ready for you. And you plant right into the cereal rye.

Now, I don’t recommend– we plant our cereal rye, and we let us get to 5, 6, 7 feet tall, and it works. So if you ever wondered how high you can get it, we let ours get about 7 feet tall, and we plant right into it.

IRA FLATOW: We like to talk about the microbiome that’s in our gut. So there’s this microbiome in the soil, too, that keeps it healthy. And that’s what you’re talking about, not ripping it up with plowing, but letting the microbiome flourish.

TODD WESTERN III: Right. Right. Exactly.

IRA FLATOW: And this is successful. The yield is successful.

TODD WESTERN III: So, yeah. So then what happens is, is that we began to see the soil health improve. And how we knew that is because every year we see less and less weeds in the field when we go to plant.

And also, you see the remnants of the cereal rye still there because we haven’t actually planted the cereal rye in the last two years for various reasons, but the natural habitation started to grow itself. And so we saw better soil health. We saw better yields. Consequently, we saw better profits.

IRA FLATOW: Wow. And how hard is it for other farmers to adopt this kind of technique?

TODD WESTERN III: I would say the biggest thing is they have to want to get the information, and the state agencies have to be able to get that information to them. And so once that information is there, there is step-by-step on how to do that.

And also, reach out to your farmers. I mean, I’m– we were the test dummy in our area. And we worked with other farmers, and it was very well.

IRA FLATOW: And you were in the papers in the headlines last December about a conference. Tell us about that.

TODD WESTERN III: So the– being that in 2017, there were only seven Black farmers in the state of Iowa. So think about that. There’s only seven Black farmers in the state of Iowa. And I knew of one other one, and that was our neighbor, Mike Cook.

So Mike Cook and the Western family were very, very close. I made some network connections with the Iowa– with the Black farmers down South. And down there, there’s 400 strong farmers down there.

And you got to remember 1944, there were 14% of the farming community was Black. Today, there’s less than 1.4%. And I dare say, 1% of that is down South. The other 0.4% is up North.

So I wanted to create a community where we knew each other, number one. Number two, to be able to share information, and number three, to be able to highlight our contributions to farming because farming transcends any race, creed, or color. It’s all hard work. And we just want to make sure–

So the Iowa Farmers of Color was put together last year. It was a success. I thought I was going to find those seven. I’m happy to say that we found over 116 farmers of color– black, white, Asian. You name it. We had it there. We had interpreters.

And it went so well that the US Secretary of Agriculture, Mr. Vilsack, came to visit with us and asked us what all the hubbub was about. And so he was very impressed with what we had. So I’m very happy about that.

\[APPLAUSE\]

IRA FLATOW: Very impressive. Very impressive. I only have a few minutes left in this segment, but I want to think about– I mentioned at the top– what the future of agriculture looks like. And Pat, let me start with you. How will– let’s say, 20, 30, 50 years from now– maybe not that far ahead.

PATRICK SCHNABEL: Yeah, I hope it’s faster than that. And what I’d like to see– the cover crops that Todd mentioned. We need to start using those more. We need to get a diversity of crops in the landscape. It’s like a retirement fund. You don’t put your entire retirement fund in one stock. You need to have some diversification to reduce risk.

So we need multiple crops in Iowa, both to reduce risk, but also so farmers can rotate multiple crops and break up disease and insect cycles. And farmers want this. They’re hungry for another crop, but we need to build the markets for that.

IRA FLATOW: And let me ask you, Todd, what do you think– because you went through six generations of families. What’s your next two generations going to see different on the farm?

TODD WESTERN III: Well, actually, I have the next generations here out in the audience. I have a 10-year-old, a 11-year-old, and a one-year-old. There they are.

\[APPLAUSE\]

So yeah. So that’s why I thought it was important for them to come to this, to see this, so that they grow into this. And the future of agriculture is just communication, platforms like this. And then I hope to grow the Iowa Farmers of Color Conference to make sure that all people of color come together in a safe space to learn from each other and to know each other.

IRA FLATOW: So you’re hopeful. I mean, a lot of people are worried about the future, but you’re sounding very hopeful.

TODD WESTERN III: You have to be hopeful. When you’re a farmer, that’s all hope, right? A farmer’s– right? It’s all hope. You throw that seed in the ground, and it’s all hope from there.

IRA FLATOW: You want to give it a little boost, though.

TODD WESTERN III: Yeah, you want to give it a little boost, but it’s a lot of hope.

IRA FLATOW: And Pat, you think the same thing?

PATRICK SCHNABEL: Absolutely. We can solve this technologically. We just have to decide to do it.

IRA FLATOW: Well, I want to thank all of you for taking time to be with us today. Todd Western III, who is a sixth-generation Iowan farmer and Senior Donor Advisor at Greater Twin Cities United Way, and Dr. Patrick Schnabel, a distinguished professor at Iowa State and co-founder of Dryland Genetics. Thank you for what you do and for taking time to be with us today.

TODD WESTERN III: Thank you.

PATRICK SCHNABEL: Thank you.

\[APPLAUSE\]

Your pantry's sweetest ingredient has an extremely bitter history. The sap-producing grass known as sugarcane has been grown and enjoyed by humans for at least 10,000 years, but it was only relatively recently that it went from a luxury to an everyday ingredient—a change that also triggered genocide, slavery, and the invention of modern racism. In this episode, how the Crusades got Europeans addicted to the sweet stuff, and how that appetite deforested southern Europe and kicked off the trade in enslaved Africans, before decimating indigenous populations in the New World and codifying racism into law. It's a dark story that involves Christopher Columbus' mistress, the early human rights advocate whose campaign to save indigenous people encouraged the horrors of the transatlantic slave trade, and a trip to southern Louisiana, where we met Black sugarcane farmers to explore sugar's troubling legacy there. No sugar coating here: join us for the fascinating and horrifying history of this household staple. Learn more about your ad choices. Visit podcastchoices.com/adchoices

Here’s a little riddle for you: What’s all around you, but can’t be seen, smelled, or tasted? Hint: It’s in your Oreos, Nutella, instant noodles, dish soap, shampoo, lipstick, potato chips, pizza dough, packaged bread, chocolate bars, ice-cream, and biodiesel. The answer is ... palm oil, the hidden ingredient on just about every aisle of the grocery store. It's the most ubiquitous, most important, most interesting oil that most of us don't really know. But palm oil wasn’t always so big, or so anonymous—in its West African homeland, it’s a fragrant red oil traditionally used in cooking and ceremonies. So how did palm oil go global? What does it have to do with the European colonization of Africa, soap for grimy factory workers, Girl Scout cookies, and Alfred Nobel of Nobel Prize-fame? How has growing demand for all things palm oil driven deforestation and peat fires in Southeast Asia—and what can we do if we want to rethink our destructive palm oil addiction? #### As cancer rates fall nationally, Iowa sees a troubling rise in diagnoses

**PBS News**, *2026-06-16*

##### Video (00:08:19)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://player.pbs.org/viralplayer/3111589187 title=As cancer rates fall nationally, Iowa sees a troubling rise in diagnoses frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

For years, national conversations about cancer have often focused on the so-called “Cancer Alley” in the Deep South or Appalachian states with high smoking rates. But recently, a different state has grabbed headlines. Iowa has the second-highest cancer incidence in the country and is one of only three states where rates are rising. Special correspondent Fred de Sam Lazaro reports.

##### Article

For years, national conversations about cancer have often focused on the so-called “Cancer Alley” in the Deep South or Appalachian states with high smoking rates. But recently, a different state has grabbed headlines. Iowa has the second-highest cancer incidence in the country and is one of only three states where rates are rising. Special correspondent Fred de Sam Lazaro reports. Amna Nawaz: For years, national conversations about cancer often focused on the so-called Cancer Alley in the Deep South or Appalachian states with high smoking rates. But, recently, a different state has grabbed headlines. Iowa. It now has the second highest cancer incidence in the country, and is one of only three states where rates are rising. Special correspondent Fred De Sam Lazaro went to Iowa and has this report on the search for answers. Fred De Sam Lazaro: For 35-year-old Becca Mataloni, it started in 2019 with a crackling noise every time she inhaled. Becca Mataloni, Iowa Resident: Kind of like dial-up Internet, is how I always describe what it sounded like. Fred De Sam Lazaro: In 2022, she developed pneumonia, in 2024, another bout of pneumonia. Mataloni, who lives in the Des Moines area, had multiple scans and met with a pulmonologist, who delivered the diagnosis, a cancerous tumor on her lung. Becca Mataloni: It's really devastating to get a cancer diagnosis in your 30s. And even though my pulmonologist told me that I was going to be OK, it sucks, and hearing I'm going to lose two-thirds of my lung. Like, one of the first questions I asked was, am I still going to be able to do the things I love? Fred De Sam Lazaro: In rural Northern Iowa, Shelley Phelps lost her sister to breast cancer in 2015. Two years later, her husband, Michael, was diagnosed with stage four colon cancer. Shelley Phelps, Iowa Resident: You think, how can I go through this again? And how can my kids go through this again? Fred De Sam Lazaro: They had to drive at least an hour any time Michael needed treatment. In 2020, he died at the age of 50. Shelley Phelps: I have always said that, if it wasn't for my faith, I would not have gotten through this, because you're always waiting for that next shoe to fall. Who's going to be diagnosed next? Fred De Sam Lazaro: The stories represent a grim reality for Iowa, which was following national cancer trends until about 2013, when rates began to rise, driven by prostate, breast and lung cancer, as well as melanoma. Now, for the third year in a row, it's got the second highest cancer incidence in the country. Its rate among young people is also near the top. As Iowa's high cancer rates have persisted in recent years, there's been growing public concern, with key unanswered questions. What's to blame for them and what are state officials doing about it? Mary Charlton, Iowa Cancer Registry: As much as we would love to reduce it down to one thing and figure this out and change Iowa's rates, we would do that. But that's not how cancer works. Fred De Sam Lazaro: Mary Charlton leads the Iowa Cancer Registry, which has tracked the state's cancer data for over 50 years. Charlton and her staff have been traveling Iowa's 99 counties, meeting with residents. Mary Charlton: A lot of people that come to the meetings have had cancer, had a loved one diagnosed with cancer, and they want to know why. That's a really maddening thing about cancer too is, people can be exposed to the same things and their immune system might process them differently. It's not an excuse to not try to figure out what's causing the cancer and do something about it, but it kind of explains why it's kind of a slow slog to figure out what's causing our rates to be higher than the rest of the country. #### Drowning in seaweed How to stop invasive Sargassum

##### Video (10:31)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/CH7MpiGCdgU title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

The story of Sargassum stretches from the Congo to the Amazon, from soybean farming to climate change and from toxic gases to robotic vehicles. In this documentary researchers from around the world explain the vast scope of the Sargassum problem and the solutions that may one day begin to address it.

Additional photographs and footage in this film were provided by Drake Lee-Patterson, Gary Marshall, Joseph Weekes, Driven Visual Media, Kerwin Noel,  Nick Hurley, Akeisha Clark, Sargassum Information Hub, NASA, Chuanmin Hu, Jeff Davis's team, Hazel Oxenford, Caroline Juang, Melvina Walsh, Morgan Lewis, Kerton Jobe, P McConney, Markel Gomez Letona and Nico Frohberg who were mistakenly missed off the film credits.

##### Transcript

**0:03** · VOICE OVER: The Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt is the largest seaweed bloom in the world, and it's expanding.

**0:11** · Visible from space, it's a growing problem for coastal communities.

**0:15** · HARSHINI VUMMADI: The beaches, genuinely, if they aren't maintained, you just can't go there.

**0:21** · You'd be up to your knees in sargassum.

**0:24** · VOICE OVER: But as a key sequester of carbon, this invasive species also presents an opportunity.

**0:30** · AJIT SUBRAMANIAM: We want to gather sargassum using robotic vehicles.

**0:34** · You sink it down 2,000 metres, our current model suggests that that particular water body does not come back in contact with the atmosphere for at least 100 years.

**0:42** · VOICE OVER: Can scientists take a global challenge and turn it into an opportunity to buy time in the race against climate change?

**1:00** · VOICE OVER: Sargassum has been in the Atlantic since the time of Christopher Columbus, floating mats of seaweed that gave its name to the Sargasso Sea – a nutrient-poor patch of the Atlantic penned in by ocean currents.

**1:13** · AJIT: You can think of it as a floating rainforest or an upside-down coral reef because each raft of sargassum is a hotspot of biological activity.

**1:22** · VOICE OVER: But in the last couple of decades, a new population has emerged, further south near the coast of Brazil and the Caribbean.

**1:29** · SHELLY-ANN COX: In 2011, we were all taken back by this new phenomenon, where we saw tons of sargassum being brought and beached in the region.

**1:42** · VOICE OVER: Based in Barbados, scientist and entrepreneur Shelly-Ann Cox specialises in fisheries management.

**1:49** · She first noticed the impact of sargassum on the sea urchin divers she was working with.

**1:54** · SHELLY-ANN: Fisher folk had reported sargassum mats as far as their eyes can see.

**2:01** · Some of them can't get to the boat or the boats can't get through the sargassum to get out.

**2:07** · Those near shore, the spear fishers as well, they reported some of their skin being irritated when they're diving and the berries that keep the sargassum floating have gotten into their ears as well.

**2:21** · VOICE OVER: The impact on tourism – the lifeblood of the Caribbean – has been huge.

**2:25** · OFF-SCREEN VOICE: This weed is going right up to the sanitation plant by Barnacle Point.

**2:33** · People, get ready for the smell tomorrow.

**2:39** · VOICE OVER: Around the same time, other scientists working in the Atlantic had also noticed a change.

**2:45** · Oceanographer Ajit Subramaniam has been working in the South Atlantic for more than 25 years.

**2:50** · AJIT: In 2018, it was astounding how much sargassum we ran into, and it was really striking.

**2:55** · It was something that we'd never seen before and then, bam.

**2:58** · We were there, and the ship was often surrounded by sargassum that was hundreds of metres around the ship.

**3:05** · VOICE OVER: Sargassum wasn't thought to be found this far south.

**3:08** · AJIT: We were seeing things that we had not seen before, and I was trying to get context for that.

**3:12** · VOICE OVER: Ajit linked up with colleagues at the University of South Florida, who had been making their own observations.

**3:17** · AJIT: They'd been actually watching this on their satellite data, and they had actually seen this explosion of this new population that is growing much closer to the equator.

**3:26** · VOICE OVER: With the satellite data, scientists were able to hazard an estimate of its size.

**3:31** · SHELLY-ANN: 24.2 million metric tons in June, from the satellite imagery.

**3:38** · VOICE OVER: Dubbed the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt, this is almost certainly the world's largest macroalgal bloom.

**3:44** · It's thought that intensive agriculture, especially soya plantations, has increased nitrogen concentrations in the Atlantic, causing rapid sargassum growth.

**3:54** · SHELLY-ANN: Sargassum is really known as a symptom of climate change because, due to increasing surface temperatures, nutrients from the Amazon and Congo, Saharan dust which brings in iron, upwelling as well, the change in currents, all of these factors have led to the proliferation of sargassum.

**4:19** · HARSHINI: Outside of the Caribbean, I don't think many people are talking about this.

**4:23** · VOICE OVER: Harshini Vummadi is a biology major undergraduate, who's recently returned from an exploratory trip to the Dominican Republic.

**4:32** · HARSHINI: It affects the Caribbean and I believe West Africa, and a bit of East Asia as well.

**4:40** · VOICE OVER: Harshini is part of an interdisciplinary team from the Georgia Institute of Technology.

**4:49** · RESEARCHER: Yeah, so, I'm just collecting some sargassum samples and there are lots of different plants in here.

**5:18** · VOICE OVER: While there are many creative small-scale craft uses of sargassum, local communities have yet to find a viable solution to disposing of vast quantities of the stuff, or even better, making it useful.

**5:30** · HARSHINI: It uptakes a lot of different heavy metals, particularly arsenic, which makes it like quite dangerous to use as, say, like a fertiliser because, again, now you're introducing arsenic to these land systems where it could potentially leach into groundwater.

**5:47** · So, we try to like branch out from fertiliser. One of our team members focused on an application involving bricks.

**6:08** · I personally have been working on using it as a bioaccumulate. Why not use it in waste water treatment?

**6:16** · It can absorb those heavy metals that we were so concerned about in the first place.

**6:21** · VOICE OVER: Harshini's team are working on ways to make the sargassum financially viable.

**6:26** · Meanwhile, Ajit is thinking more broadly, exploring the bigger checks and balances of the global carbon cycle.

**6:32** · He's come up with a radical plan.

**6:34** · AJIT: So, the way we want to do this is essentially gather nets of sargassum using robotic vehicles, have them ballasted and then sink them down to 2,000 metres.

**6:46** · VOICE OVER: Sargassum sequesters a lot of carbon, but it also releases it when it decays.

**6:52** · This approach would theoretically remove the carbon from the atmosphere, effectively buying the planet time in the race against climate change.

**6:59** · AJIT: Sinking down 2,000 metres, our current model suggests that that particular water body does not come back in contact with the atmosphere for at least 100 years.

**7:08** · VOICE OVER: The idea of sinking the sargassum has been proposed before, but the suggestion is usually to sink it where it grows, in shallower water.

**7:15** · AJIT: Merely capturing it at the surface and getting rid of it just off the beach at 100 metres or something like that will basically have the carbon coming right back up.

**7:46** · VOICE OVER: In addition, as a biologist, he's keen to understand the impact of this plan on the ecosystem.

**7:51** · AJIT: So, we actually have a fisheries scientist on the team who will be looking at what kind of communities the sargassum rafts harbour, and therefore we'll have a sense of what we might be impacting if we were to do the sinking.

**8:02** · It's not that we're going to decimate the ocean of sargassum.

**8:06** · VOICE OVER: The list of problems attributed to sargassum is growing. From the harmful gases released when it decays to its impact on wildlife.

**8:28** · SHELLY-ANN: So, every year we're seeing more countries reporting the influx and the catastrophic impacts on tourism, fisheries sectors, maritime and transport and then the health impacts.

Watch more of this series: https://to.pbs.org/4wkQIAG

The Colorado River is running out — and the Imperial Valley is ground zero. As policymakers battle over rights to a shrinking river, farmers are grappling with the practical realities of growing food with less water. Miles O’Brien meets two Imperial Valley farmers who are finding ways to feed people and livestock, nearby and abroad, while trying to make good use of every drop of this hard-working river.

#### How FIVE BILLION Pounds of Las Vegas Garbage Powers a City

**PBS Terra**, *04 20, 2021*

##### Video (9:14)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/aHzltu6Tvl8 title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

PBS Member Stations rely on viewers like you. To support your local station, go to: http://to.pbs.org/DonateTerra

Head over to Reactions to find out more about how they're celebrating Earth Day, and tell them Joe sent you! https://youtu.be/I1YLPfSuNXY

Most of the 600 billion pounds of waste that Americans produce every year ends up in landfills. All that trash can have huge impacts on the environment. But modern landfills have found a new use for all that trash — they’re turning it into energy. In spite of their reputation as “dumps,” these landfills are feats of engineering, more akin to construction sites. 

One of North America’s biggest landfills lies on the outskirts of Las Vegas. The Apex Landfill is not only one of the country’s largest, it’s also one of the busiest. Because it serves a non-stop city, the landfill must operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. It receives upwards of 16 million pounds of trash per day or 5 billion pounds per year.  

Landfills like Apex are required to deal with the toxic chemicals they produce, like methane, a greenhouse gas that’s 84 times more potent than carbon dioxide. At Apex, they capture that methane and turn it into energy that powers 11,000 homes in southern Nevada.

Las Vegas produces more than five billion pounds of waste per year, and all that trash ends up here. The Apex Landfill lies in the mountains beyond the city.

###### Apex Landfill

**1:12** · At 1900 acres, it's one of the largest landfills in North America, and also one of the busiest. Apex is one of the only landfills in North America that runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week, 365 days a year. **1:46** · trash dumped in piles with little regard for sanitation. As trash decays, it produces methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. ###### Working Phase


**2:33** · [David]: The working face is the active area of the landfill, usually anywhere from two to three acres in size.

**2:57** · [David]: Each one of those machines is about 120 to 130,000 pounds. There's a lot of weight that will smash all the cardboard boxes or trash or any other material that comes in. **3:24** · [Joe]: As more and more trash comes in, the landfill grows in height.

**3:29** · [David]: It's just like building a pyramid. The wider the base, the higher we can go with the trash here in the landfill.

**3:36** · [Joe]: In some areas, the local landfill is the highest point in the region. Here in Vegas, this mountain of trash is 500 feet high and rising taller by the day. In spite of the enormous volume of garbage coming in, the landfill will be able to take in trash for another 300 plus years.

**4:01** · Not only is the site large, but it's also growing. A mining company on site digs out the surrounding mountains. Las Vegas boasts the largest residential recycling center in North America. The state-of-the-art facility takes in up to 1.8 million pounds of recyclables per day.

###### Recycling

**4:32** · Because Las Vegas uses single stream recycling, all the sorting happens here. These recyclables will get conveyed through a complex system of sorting machines.

**4:45** · [Jeremy Walters]: We have some very unique pieces of equipment, things that do just simple mechanical separation through disks and screens, but we also have computerized machines that are physically reading the material based on its color and density. It's very smart, and it's very quick. After a machine initially separates material, people quality control what the machine did.

Some landfills capture and burn it. But here at Apex, and at a growing number of landfills around the country, they're turning it into energy. 160 wells have been drilled into this mountain of trash, some as deep as 200 feet.

**7:31** · The wells siphon off the gas coming from landfill. After it's purified, it's sent to an onsite power plant where it's burned to spin turbines, which create energy. #### Mexico’s Caribbean beaches overwhelmed by record sargassum influx I Inside Latin America

**Al Jazeera English**, *09 05, 2026*

##### Video (10:02)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/6PHfReEbjcA title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

The Caribbean is facing a growing sargassum seaweed crisis, with huge quantities washing onto beaches across the region and threatening tourism, ecosystems and public health.

Mexico’s Riviera Maya has been particularly affected, with the influx reaching thousands of tonnes of seaweed each day.

As the algae decomposes on beaches, it can release toxic gases, raising health concerns for residents and tourists. Scientists also warn that the accumulation of sargassum can damage seagrass ecosystems and affect beach stability.

The crisis is putting pressure on Mexico’s tourism industry, while the Mexican Navy has stepped up efforts to collect the seaweed before it reaches the shore.

But some businesses are looking at sargassum differently.

Companies including Carbonwave and Sargablock are developing ways to transform the invasive algae into products such as bio-fertilizers, footwear and construction materials.

Could an environmental crisis become a new source of sustainable materials?

##### Transcript

**0:04** · [music] Welcome to Inside Latin America and to Mexico's Riviera Maya. For the last decade, growing amounts of algae called sargassum have been washing up on beaches across the Caribbean, transforming once pristine coastlines and threatening the communities that depend on them.

#### WHO Preventing disease through healthy environments

**World Health Organization (WHO)**, *04 20, 2016*

##### Video (2:00)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/tupJDf13jBo title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

An estimated 12.6 million people died as a result of living or working in an unhealthy environment in 2012 – nearly 1 in 4 of total global deaths, according to the World Health Organization. Environmental risk factors, such as air, water and soil pollution, chemical exposures, climate change, and ultraviolet radiation, contribute to more than 100 diseases and injuries. However, we can take actions to reverse the upward trend of environment-related diseases and improve our environments where we live and work.
 
For more information visit: http://who.int/quantifying_ehimpacts/publications/preventing-disease/en/

#### Why don’t we just burn our trash

**DW Planet A**, *08 13, 2021*

##### Video (10:45)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/OPVUrO-_7SM title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Waste to energy plants are seen as green innovations for countries where landfills dominate, as they reduce methane and generate renewable energy. But will these incinerators really make our trash problems go up in flames?

We're destroying our environment at an alarming rate. But it doesn't need to be this way. Our new channel Planet A explores the shift towards an eco-friendly world — and challenges our ideas about what dealing with climate change means. We look at the big and the small: What we can do and how the system needs to change. Every Friday we'll take a truly global look at how to get us out of this mess.

###### Intro

**0:01** · These skiers are all here because of trash.

**0:05** · That’s because underneath this slope is a huge garbage incineration plant.

**0:10** · It processes 400,000 metric tons of waste a year and turns it into energy and heat for Copenhagen.

**0:18** · It also recycles 90% of the city’s metal waste.

**0:22** · Some say such incineration plants could be key for solving our global trash problem.

**0:28** · But is that true?

**0:30** · Or are we going to end up just getting burned?

###### Why we need better waste management

**0:39** · Globally, we produce over two billion tons of household waste annually, with high income countries generating an outsized amount compared to their populations.

**0:50** · 37% of global waste ends up in landfills, polluting groundwater and producing methane.

**0:57** · Less than 20% of the world’s trash is recycled or composted.

**1:02** · In the Global South many people have no access to trash collection, and it often ends up in rivers — a primary source of ocean plastic.

**1:12** · To get rid of as much trash as possible, as fast as possible, around one billion tons of waste are openly burned every year.

**1:22** · "Open burning generates high levels of black carbon, which is soot, which has a really strong global warming effect."

**1:31** · Zoë Lenkiewicz is one of the founding members of Wasteaid, and has been a waste manager for over 20 years.

**1:38** · “It also generates dioxins and furans, which are known to cause cancer.

**1:41** · All of this is going into the local air, wherever people are burning waste.”

**1:48** · Women are more directly impacted, as they are often responsible for disposing of household waste.

**1:53** · Burning trash this way is a serious problem. But done differently, there are advantages to it.

###### Waste to energy

**2:01** · Here’s where controlled burning, aka incineration, comes in.

**2:04** · Incinerators first appeared where it was hard to landfill, in London in 1874, then in New York City, in 1885.

**2:12** · “The incineration process itself, it reduces the volume of the waste [by] 90 percent.”

**2:19** · Ella Stengler is the managing director of the umbrella organization for European waste to energy operators.

**2:25** · “And it fulfills the kind of sanitary task because it destroys the pollutants which are embedded in the waste.”

**2:32** · The generated heat can also be turned into energy. It's called, unsurprisingly, waste to energy.

**2:38** · In the US, where there’s a lot of space and cheap energy in the form of oil, waste to energy wasn’t so competitive, and many plants were closed.

**2:46** · But more and more plants were built in the EU.

**2:50** · Today they provide power to 18 million Europeans, and heat to 15 million.

**2:56** · They’re a common waste management option for countries like Denmark and the Netherlands, which have almost completely eliminated landfilling.

**3:05** · Environmental organizations see potential in waste to energy as a transition step toward a more circular economy, especially in countries without much space, that need more energy.

**3:18** · Here’s how the plants work: The garbage is dumped into a big pit — from there it’s fed into the furnaces.

**3:25** · They burn extremely hot, and the waste is reduced in a matter of minutes.

**3:30** · The heat from the fires generates steam, which turns turbines to create electricity.

**3:35** · The steam can also be used for heating.

**3:38** · The 10% that doesn’t burn is called bottom ash, and metals can be recovered from it.

**3:44** · The rest can then be used as construction material.

**3:50** · So the process reduces the volume of waste, creates energy, and part of the residue can even be recycled.

**3:58** · What’s not to love?

**4:01** · Well, there are a few reasons why the world isn’t full of waste to energy plants with ski slopes on top.

**4:07** · One of those reasons is fly ash, which is everything caught by the filters.

**4:11** · It needs to be disposed of in a hazardous waste facility.

**4:15** · Another reason is cost.

**4:16** · “If there would be a waste to energy plant built, it should be equipped with a state-of-the-art technology, which is expensive.

**4:27** · And you need to train the staff to properly operate it and also authorities to monitor it.”

**4:33** · Even without ski slopes, waste to energy plants can cost over one billion US dollars to build.

**4:39** · Without the latest technology and monitoring, pollution can reach unsafe levels, and impact people living nearby.

**4:47** · And they also emit a lot of CO2: in the EU, around 52 million tonnes per year.

**4:56** · That’s like 430,000 cars each driving a million kilometers.

**5:02** · “Policymakers and industries put incineration in the same type of energy group as renewables, like wind or solar or even nuclear."

**5:15** · This is Tatiana Lujan.

**5:16** · She leads the plastics team for ClientEarth, and is also working to implement the EU's circular economy directive.

**5:24** · “But when you look at the greenhouse gas emissions of incineration, they're actually pretty close to coal and gas, and way far from wind, solar, nuclear.

**5:36** · A study commissioned by ClientEarth found that controlled incineration generates between 59 and 73% of the emissions that coal would.

**5:44** · Classifying this energy as renewable can divert funding from more sustainable waste management technologies like recycling.

**5:51** · So, where it can be correctly built and managed, controlled incineration is better than a landfill – but it’s by far not the cleanest option to handle waste, no matter how much energy is won.

###### The Waste Hierarchy

**6:04** · Have a look at this “waste hierarchy pyramid” – bear with me, it’s less complicated than it looks.

**6:09** · At the very bottom of the pyramid is open burning or dumping, the worst possible way to get rid of trash.

**6:15** · Disposal without energy recovery is next, so landfilling or incineration without energy generation.

**6:22** · Then here’s where waste to energy, which is an umbrella term for a few different methods, comes in.

**6:29** · Then comes recycling.

**6:31** · Even better is to re-use things, often called upcycling, and at the top is prevention and reduction.

**6:38** · Yeah, the whole world is pretty far from the top.

**6:42** · That is why waste to energy is seen by some as a quick “solution” for countries struggling with their waste.

###### A waste solution for the Global South?

**6:51** · Not surprisingly, plants are opening up around the world, like in China, Indonesia and India.

**7:02** · Africa’s first waste to energy plant just opened, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

**7:08** · But it has proven to be more complicated than just opening up plants and burning the problem away.

**7:14** · One reason is that the composition of waste varies widely throughout the world.

**7:22** · “You can't take one model that works in a wealthy country like a cookie cutter and expect it to work in a low-income country because it's a completely different market.”

**7:34** · In India, household waste is around 50 percent organic matter, like food scraps, which are too wet to burn.

**7:41** · And because of the lack of centralized waste collection, trash there is often mixed together.

**7:48** · “I don't think segregation is happening at all in majority of the Indian cities.

**7:55** · So that's a major, major problem.”

**7:57** · Pritpal Randhawa has been conducting long-term studies on waste management in India for the past 10 years.

**8:02** · “The waste has to be segregated and the undesirable material should be separated from that waste, and only the waste with high calorific value should be burned.

**8:14** · But that is not something which is happening actually.”

**8:18** · Calorific value is a measure of a substance’s heating power — in other words, how easily it burns.

**8:24** · Crude oil and mixed plastics come in at around 40 megajoules per kilogram.

**8:29** · Food is about 16.

**8:31** · Without waste separation, lots of food scraps find their way to the furnaces, forcing the plants to add additional fuel.

**8:39** · This makes the whole facility extremely inefficient.

**8:42** · Countries also need to have a place to store the hazardous waste.

**8:46** · So if incineration isn’t a silver bullet for the Global South, what are other options?

**8:52** · “It’s not very complicated at all – the ideal situation would be management of waste at the decentralized level.”

**9:01** · And not only decentral, but diversified: specifically suited to the environment and economy of an area.

**9:10** · In many cities in India, for example, waste pickers collect recyclables, which are processed informally.

**9:15** · Biogas generated from organic waste can be a source of fuel from Benin to Mumbai.

**9:20** · And plastic can be made into building material.

**9:25** · “With waste management, absolutely one size does not fit all.

**9:28** · And you really need to look at what's most appropriate for that local area.”

###### When incineration makes sense

**9:34** · Waste to energy plants can work, but a trash collection system and a strong environmental regulator are both necessary.

**9:41** · These can be really hard to come by.

**9:44** · Even with them, countries need to do some careful reflection before building new plants.

**9:48** · “When you create incineration, you're making huge investments and locking yourself in a system that you're going to have to continue feeding and feeding and feeding.

**10:00** · And that creates a disincentive for transitioning to a real circular economy.”

**10:08** · So before more trash burning facilities join the global system, policymakers should look at funding more sustainable methods of waste disposal – like recycling, reusing and most importantly, reducing our waste in the first place.
